clue.text: Drop is put into drink

indicators.note: something put into another thing ends up inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
to down a drink is to swallow it

explanation.surface: Somebody's tipple has had something dropped into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop' looks like a noun, a drop of drink, but it is the verb meaning abandon; 'drink' is the verb too, to swallow.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop someone in the sense of abandoning or repudiating them is to disown them.

clue.text: Section in contract withdrawn

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other, as a clause sits within a document

blocks.note: a bit is a section or part
a deed is a legal contract

explanation.surface: A clause of an agreement has been pulled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' tempts as the verb meaning shrink; it is the noun, a legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: Money debited from an account has been withdrawn or taken out of it.

clue.text: Remove untidy vegetation

blocks.note: first meaning: to cancel or delete, as in scrubbing a plan
second meaning: rough, stunted bushes and undergrowth

explanation.surface: An instruction to clear away a scruffy patch of plants.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an informal verb for cancelling something and a noun for straggly low-growing shrubland.

clue.text: See 14
Oxygen-fuelled lifting device found after little time – not long?

indicators.note: a machine that is fuelled has its fuel put inside it
found after places one piece behind the other in reading order

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
a winch hauls loads up

explanation.surface: A crane running on oxygen turns up shortly afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes inside WINCH, after its W, and T stands in front: T-W-O-INCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Something only two inches in length is short, hence the question mark on a definition by example.

clue.text: Insolence shown after performance: Congress let it go

indicators.note: shown after puts the first-named piece at the end, behind the others

blocks.note: a turn is a performer's act on stage
congress in its sense of sex
cheek is rude impudence

explanation.surface: After a rude display, a legislature decides to drop the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' looks like the US legislature but means sexual intercourse, which British slang calls 'the other'.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn the other cheek is to refuse to retaliate, letting an offence pass without response.

clue.text: See 4
Short investigation into fruit served up for a piece of cake

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the word loses its final letter
in a down clue, served up means the word is read from bottom to top
into places one piece within the other

blocks.note: a probe is an inquiry
a melon is a fruit

explanation.surface: A brief inquiry into fruit, offered as dessert alongside cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served up' suits the dessert picture, but in a down clue it turns the fruit upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of cake is an idiom for something easy, which is exactly what no problem describes.

clue.text: String runs through pipes

indicators.note: something running through another passes inside it

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
hoses are flexible pipes

explanation.surface: A cord is threaded down some tubing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String' looks like cord, but it is a trainer's string, the set of racehorses in one stable.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing stable's string is the group of horses it trains, so horses can stand for a string.

clue.text: *one* flight

indicators.note: the word one is printed with a symbol on either side of it, so it sits between them

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
asterisks are typographic stars, and two of them flank the word

explanation.surface: A single journey by air, emphasised.
explanation.walkthrough: The asterisks are part of the wordplay: an asterisk is a star, so this is one inside STARS. Fifteensquared commenters noted the markup is an old convention for bold, which hides the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight is a set of steps between floors, so the plural noun stairs matches it.

clue.text: Gentleman sent back in exchange for lawyer

indicators.note: something sent back goes the other way, so the word is read from the end
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: sir is the title for a gentleman
to barter is to trade goods in exchange

explanation.surface: A man is returned as part of a swap for a lawyer, like a prisoner trade.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a barrister is the kind of lawyer who argues cases in court, as distinct from a solicitor.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrister is a British courtroom lawyer, the kind qualified to argue cases in the higher courts.

clue.text: Excitable, somewhat touchy perhaps

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: the run of letters across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: A description of an irritable, jumpy personality.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyper is an informal adjective for someone overexcited and highly strung.

clue.text: See 28
Cook tries open sandwich

indicators.note: to cook something is to cook the books, rigging and rearranging it

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A kitchen instruction to make an open sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwich' looks like a noun in the kitchen picture, but it is the verb meaning to put something between two others.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpose is to place something between other things, which is what sandwiching does.

clue.text: It becomes more peaceful for wild animals

blocks.note: when the noise departs, a place grows quieter

explanation.surface: Some state of affairs turns out calmer for creatures in the wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as a scene: things become more peaceful when the din goes. Split DIN GOES differently and it is DINGOES.
explanation.definitionFit: Dingoes are the wild dogs of Australia, untamed animals.

clue.text: Average postcard unnecessary then?

blocks.note: surface reading: an ordinary, run-of-the-mill holiday card
setter's reading: if a postcard is not needed, there is no news worth sending to the family

explanation.surface: Someone decides an ordinary postcard is not worth sending.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is taken literally: no postcard is needed when there is no news.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something unremarkable or mediocre, which is what average means.

clue.text: Hands down back of settee, a number of items not quite retrieved, unknown quantity

indicators.note: back of means only the final letter of the word is kept
not quite means the word falls just short, losing its last letter
retrieved is read as re-, back, so the word is turned round

blocks.note: the last letter of settee
taken as written
a list is a set of items
algebra uses Y for an unknown

explanation.surface: Someone digs behind the sofa cushions and comes up with a few lost things.
explanation.walkthrough: LIST loses its T, then the remaining LIS is turned round. 'Hands down' looks like part of the rummaging but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning hands down means winning with no effort at all, which is to win easily.

clue.text: Cock-up over character without children

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom to the top
over in a down clue puts the first piece above the second

blocks.note: cock is slang for the male organ
a role is a character in a play

explanation.surface: A blunder over a part means someone is left childless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cock-up' is British slang for a blunder, but here it is split: cock, then up as the reversal signal. Sine prole is a Latin legal phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Sine prole is legal Latin meaning without issue, used in genealogies for people who died childless.

clue.text: Leader in Russian preserved by a paper, still

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
something preserved is kept enclosed, held within the other piece

blocks.note: the first letter of Russian
a paper is an exam, a test

explanation.surface: A Russian figurehead kept safe by some newspaper, even now.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside A TEST. 'Paper' suggests a newspaper, but it is an exam paper; 'still' looks like 'even now' but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at rest is motionless, the adjectival sense of still.

clue.text: As requested, 19 down pulled up?

indicators.note: a plant pulled up comes out of the ground, and in a down clue up means read bottom to top

blocks.note: the answer to 19 down, a radish, is a red root

explanation.surface: A vegetable from another clue is harvested on request.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is not replaced by its answer but by a description of it: a radish is a red root.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made to order is made as the customer asked, as requested.

clue.text: A cruciverbalist residing in Split given new identity

indicators.note: someone residing in a place lives inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter, a crossword compiler, refers to himself as me
to rend is to tear apart

explanation.surface: A crossword setter living in the Croatian city of Split takes on a fresh name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' looks like the Croatian city, but it is the verb for tearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone renamed has been given a different name and so a new identity.

clue.text: Edible plant, a food under review, originally

indicators.note: originally points to the beginning, the opening letter of the word
under in a down clue puts the earlier pieces below the last one

blocks.note: the first letter of review
taken as written
a dish is food served at a meal

explanation.surface: A restaurant critic is assessing a vegetable dish.
explanation.definitionFit: The radish is a plant grown for its peppery edible root.

clue.text: Follow communist, gentle pace

blocks.note: to dog someone is to tail them
Trot is short for a Trotskyist

explanation.surface: An instruction to tail a left-winger at an easy walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogtrot is a gentle, easy-going trot, a slow steady pace.

clue.text: Pants, where fire breaks out in lying?

indicators.note: a fire breaking out spreads wildly, so its letters scatter into a new order
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
BS, short for bullshit, is lying nonsense

explanation.surface: A nod to the playground chant 'liar, liar, pants on fire'.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English 'pants' are underpants, which is why briefs fit; BS is a coarse abbreviation for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Briefs are close-fitting underpants, which British English calls pants.

clue.text: Travelling in car, thunderous – if so, what's up?

indicators.note: travelling means moving about, so these letters move into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
thunderous means very loud

explanation.surface: A noisy drive prompts the question of what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'what's up' literally: if there is thunder, the thing overhead in the sky is a rain cloud.
explanation.definitionFit: A rain cloud is what hangs up in the sky in thundery weather, so it answers the literal question.

clue.text: See 4
Bump on the rear sounded – little accident

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its tail end, so only its final letter is kept

blocks.note: the last letter of bump
a bell that sounded rang

explanation.surface: A minor knock to the back of a car, with a bang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bump' looks like the definition of a minor crash, but only its final letter is used. A prang is British slang for a minor collision.
explanation.definitionFit: A prang is informal British for a minor crash, especially a small car accident.

clue.text: See 14
Hunter with shaved head, one might be bald

indicators.note: a shaved head has lost its top, so the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: the beagle is a hunting hound

explanation.surface: A hunter with a shaven scalp could be mistaken for being bald.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bald' seems to follow on from the shaved head, but it names the American bald eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: The bald eagle is a well-known species, so an eagle is something that might be bald.

clue.text: Shame miserable clothing is being worn by husband

indicators.note: clothing wraps around a body, so one piece encloses the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
something worn by a husband is on him: H, the abbreviation for husband, carrying ON
dour means gloomy

explanation.surface: A man is humiliated by wearing drab clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Something worn by a husband is on him, so the husband's H comes first with ON after it; the gloomy word then wraps around the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishonour is disgrace or loss of respect, so it is a synonym of shame.

clue.text: Corner insert fit for pocketed item?

indicators.note: insert is read as two parts, in plus the rest, and in places the first piece inside the rest

blocks.note: a nook is a corner
insert read as in plus sert: in is the container signal, and the remaining letters are kept
fit to do something means able to do it

explanation.surface: An instruction to fit a corner piece, perhaps on something with pockets.
explanation.walkthrough: The word insert is split as in plus SERT. 'Corner' itself means snooker, a red herring for anyone hunting the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A snooker table has six pockets for the balls, so it is an item fitted with pockets.

clue.text: Balance at the limits having sex on your bike!

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its two ends, its outer letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of balance
couples at it are having sex

explanation.surface: A cyclist steadies their balance while getting amorous in the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On your bike' is British slang for go away; it is the definition, not a cycling scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat it and on your bike are both slangy commands telling someone to leave.
